claims.text: Helm is a graduated Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF) project.
Helm is open source under the Apache License 2.0 and the Helm project does not ship a commercial tier.
The `helm` CLI renders chart templates using Go template syntax and either installs the resulting manifests into a cluster as a release or prints them to stdout.
Helm charts are indexed publicly on Artifact Hub.
In Pulumi, resource ordering is derived from the dependency graph: each resource waits for its dependencies to become ready, and independent resources deploy in parallel.

Helm applies resources in a fixed order by Kubernetes kind (defined in helm/helm pkg/release/v1/util/kind_sorter.go); chart authors can't declare dependencies between resources or subcharts, except through hook weights.
Helm doesn't let a chart author declare that one resource depends on another.

The Helm docs state that "the Kubernetes objects from the charts and all its dependencies are aggregated into a single set; then sorted by type followed by name; and then created/updated in that order."

Helm's install order is a hardcoded list of Kubernetes kinds in the Helm source, beginning with PriorityClasses and Namespaces, then Secrets and ConfigMaps, then CustomResourceDefinitions and RBAC, then Services and workloads, with any kind not on the list (including custom resources) last.
Helm uninstall runs the same kind-ordered list in reverse.
Helm sends the sorted manifests to the API server in a single pass and doesn't wait for one resource to become ready before applying the next.

Helm chart dependencies don't change resource ordering: a subchart's objects are merged into the parent chart's set and sorted by kind, so a chart can't express installing one subchart before another or starting a Deployment after a Job completes.
Helm chart hooks ordered with `helm.sh/hook-weight` annotations are a workaround for ordering, and the hook resources are not managed by Helm as part of the release.
Native sequencing for resources and subcharts in Helm has been proposed in HIP-0025, which is still a draft.
In Pulumi, passing one resource's output into another or setting the `dependsOn` resource option creates an edge in the dependency graph used for ordering.
The Pulumi Kubernetes provider waits for each resource to become ready before creating the resources that depend on it, and deploys independent resources in parallel.
Pulumi deletes resources following the dependency graph in reverse.
Pulumi's dependency-graph ordering with parallel deployment makes updates faster than a strict serial sequence.

The Pulumi Kubernetes `helm.v4.Chart` resource supports the `config.kubernetes.io/depends-on` annotation for ordering between objects inside the chart, and `dependsOn` on the chart for dependencies on resources outside it.
Helm records each install or upgrade as a numbered release revision and `helm rollback` restores a prior revision.
A failed Pulumi update leaves the stack partially updated, and users roll forward by reverting program code and running `pulumi up`.
Helm favors fast revision-based rollback of a single release; Pulumi favors scriptable control over resources from many providers in one update.
Helm and Pulumi are commonly used in combination rather than as substitutes.
Two patterns cover most production deployments of using Pulumi and Helm together.
Pulumi can install cert-manager, ingress-nginx, and external-dns through `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release`.
When Pulumi outputs are passed into a chart's `values` input, Pulumi resolves the values at deploy time and orders the chart install after its dependencies.
The page has an FAQ section titled "What's the difference between `helm.Chart` and `helm.Release`?" with anchor #whats-the-difference-between-helmchart-and-helmrelease.
Pulumi creates and deletes resources in dependency order, with each resource ready before the ones that depend on it, rather than in a fixed order by kind.
There are three common ways to adopt Pulumi alongside or in place of Helm.
Using Helm charts directly from a Pulumi program with `helm.v4.Chart` or `helm.v3.Release` is the most common adoption pattern.
Charts can be converted to native Pulumi code by rendering with `helm template` and converting the YAML with `pulumi convert --from kubernetes`.
`pulumi import` and the `import` resource option generate the corresponding code for imported in-cluster resources.
A Pulumi program can pull charts from any Helm repository (public or private), and pass values as typed Pulumi inputs including outputs from other resources.
`helm.v4.Chart` renders chart templates locally and registers each Kubernetes object as an individual Pulumi resource, so every child shows up in plan output, drift detection, and state.
`helm.v3.Release` uses the embedded Helm SDK and creates a real Helm release in the cluster, preserving chart hooks, post-rendering, and release history.

Helm merges objects from a chart and all its dependencies into a single set, sorts them by Kubernetes kind, and applies them in that order, so declaring a subchart as a dependency doesn't make it install first.
Pulumi's chart `values` input accepts the same shape as a `values.yaml` file but lets each leaf be a Pulumi output; Pulumi installs the chart after the resources it depends on.
